site.title: ML + Theory Seminar
site.audience: Anyone with an interest in ML and CS Theory

talks.speaker: Jui Chien Lin
talks.title: SNAP-KG: Streaming Node Assignment via Projection for Knowledge Graph Entity Integration
talks.abstract: Knowledge graph construction must continuously integrate new entities into a growing graph, but newly arriving entities have no connectivity and cannot be assigned to communities by transductive clustering methods without retraining. We propose SNAP-KG, a graph-structural multi-view clustering framework for streaming knowledge graph entities that learns a projector network to map each new entity from its raw features directly into the embedding space, enabling immediate cluster assignment without graph access or retraining. This inductive design supports continuous ingestion while preserving relational structure, and it can be used to scope downstream entity resolution and link prediction to a much smaller candidate set. Experiments on five benchmark multi-view graph datasets and a production-scale KG with 2.4 million nodes show order-of-magnitude inference speedups over retraining-based methods and competitive clustering quality, with 62-75% candidate search reduction for downstream tasks.
talks.short_abstract: An inductive multi-view KG clustering framework for streaming entities that speeds up cluster assignment and candidate scoping.

talks.speaker: Md Saikat Islam Khan Bappy
talks.title: FedV-KGQA: Multi-Hop Question Answering over Vertically Partitioned Knowledge Graphs
talks.format: Practice talk for accepted ISWC 2026 paper
talks.abstract: Knowledge graph question answering often spans organizations that cannot share raw data because of governance and data sovereignty constraints. We propose FedV-KGQA, a framework for multi-hop reasoning over vertically partitioned knowledge graphs in which organizations share entities but keep disjoint sets of relations. The method combines local graph enrichment, knowledge graph embeddings, and a topic entity anchoring mechanism so raw triples and relation parameters never leave a silo and no runtime inter-silo communication is needed. Across three benchmarks and 12 model configurations, FedV-KGQA stays close to centralized performance, generalizes to 3-hop reasoning, and remains robust to embedding perturbations.
talks.short_abstract: A federated multi-hop KGQA framework for vertically partitioned knowledge graphs that preserves silo boundaries and stays close to centralized performance.

talks.speaker: Maruf Ahmed Mridul
talks.title: GrOIL: Graph-Grounded Domain Ontology Induction with Constrained LLM Mediation
talks.format: Practice talk for accepted CIKM 2026 paper
talks.abstract: Constructing formal ontologies from domain documents requires corpus grounding, vocabulary consistency, axiom-level expressivity, and end-to-end provenance. We present a seven-stage graph-grounded pipeline that converts domain documents into a complete, auditable OWL Terminological Box (TBox) without any unconstrained generation step. Documents are first encoded as Unified Discourse-Hypergraphs (UDH) that capture entity participation and discourse dependencies, and later stages transform this evidence into a class hierarchy, typed object and datatype properties, and restriction axioms while limiting LLM use to narrow, graph-grounded mediation tasks. A paired Assertional Box (ABox) population procedure grounds named individuals and enables SPARQL-based functional evaluation. On the life insurance domain, using two established benchmarks and a new 100-contract corpus spanning ten product types, the pipeline outperforms direct and multi-agent LLM baselines on competency-question coverage, keyphrase coverage, and structured gap-and-overlap reasoning while requiring no manual TBox engineering.
talks.short_abstract: A graph-grounded ontology induction pipeline that builds auditable OWL TBoxes from domain documents with constrained LLM mediation.

talks.speaker: Christopher Okonkwo
talks.title: Machine Unlearning for Large Language Models: Concepts, Methods, and Challenges
talks.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on massive, heterogeneous corpora inevitably absorb sensitive, copyrighted, or hazardous information, raising critical concerns around privacy, safety, and regulatory compliance. Machine unlearning aims to selectively remove such knowledge from trained models while preserving overall utility, yet remains theoretically underdeveloped and empirically fragile. This talk presents a structured study of machine unlearning for LLMs, introducing a formal problem setup and a unifying taxonomy that organizes existing approaches by intervention layer: weight-space optimization methods, representation-level and localized edits, logit-space and output-distribution manipulation, and causal or distributional alignment frameworks. We analyze how these methods instantiate forget-retain objectives, and the degree to which they achieve approximate versus retraining-equivalent unlearning. Through an empirical synthesis of results across widely used benchmarks (e.g., TOFU, WMDP, PKU-SafeRLHF, and copyright datasets), we show that many reported gains rely on narrow behavioral proxies that fail to capture true knowledge removal.
talks.short_abstract: A structured survey of machine unlearning for LLMs, with a taxonomy of intervention layers and a critique of common evaluation proxies.

talks.speaker: Thomas Waite
talks.title: Statistical-Symbolic Verification of Perception-Based Autonomous Systems using State-Dependent Conformal Prediction
talks.abstract: Reachability analysis is a standard tool for providing safety guarantees for neurally controlled autonomous systems, but its direct application to neural perception components is infeasible due to imperfect or intractable perception models. A common workaround is to combine symbolic reachability with statistical bounds on perception error, for example via conformal prediction (CP). However, existing CP methods for time-series data often produce conservative error bounds, and the resulting accumulation of uncertainty over time makes it difficult to integrate statistical guarantees with reachability analysis in a provable, scalable, and minimally conservative way. This talk introduces state-dependent conformal prediction, based on the key observation that perception error varies significantly with the system's dynamical state. We exploit this dependency to construct tighter high-confidence error bounds by partitioning the state space using a genetic algorithm that optimizes conformal tightness. Incorporating these bounds into reachability analysis induces additional branching and uncertainty, so we further propose a branch-merging reachability algorithm that trades controlled uncertainty for scalability. Empirical results on two complementary case studies demonstrate substantially reduced conservatism compared to existing verification approaches.
talks.short_abstract: Combines state-dependent conformal prediction with symbolic reachability to reduce conservatism in safety verification for perception-based autonomous systems.

talks.speaker: Prof. Chen Wang
talks.title: Adversarial Online Learning with Limited Feedback and Memory
talks.abstract: While classical MWU and EXP3 algorithms for online learning and adversarial bandits achieve \(\sqrt{T}\,\mathrm{poly}(n)\) regret, they require \(O(n \log T)\) space to implement, which is inefficient for modern large-scale applications. Recent work by Srinivas et al. (STOC 2022), Peng and Zhang (SODA 2023), and Peng and Rubinstein (FOCS 2023) established polylogarithmic-memory algorithms for the full-feedback setting (\(q = n\), where \(q\) is the number of experts/bandits queried at each step), but the limited-feedback case (\(q < n\)) remained open. This talk presents the first algorithms achieving \(o(T)\) regret with \(o(n)\) memory for \(q < n\), using only \(\tilde{O}(\mathrm{polylog}(nT))\) memory. The results include: (i) a \(T^{2/3}\) regret bound for the \(q = 1\) bandit case, improvable to the optimal \(\sqrt{nT}\) under random-order losses; (ii) a near-optimal \(\sqrt{nT}\) regret bound for \(q = 2\); and (iii) extensions to interval regret and sliding-window models. The main techniques use estimated bandit losses for pool management and a separation of exploration and exploitation to remove dependency for boosting. These techniques may be of independent interest.
talks.short_abstract: New memory-efficient adversarial online learning algorithms for the limited-feedback regime \(q < n\), with regret bounds near the best possible rates.

talks.speaker: Deniz Koyuncu
talks.title: Misleading without Lying: Adversarial Missingness Attacks
talks.abstract: Machine learning models frequently operate on datasets with missing entries, often struggling with the inherent bias this introduces. While missing data is traditionally attributed to benign collection errors, the rise of multi-source, unvetted datasets introduces a new threat: adversarial missingness. In this talk, I will define this class of attacks and discuss the theoretical feasibility of missing data attacks on causal structure learning. I will then demonstrate how to design finite-data efficient attacks by framing the challenge as a bi-level optimization problem. Finally, I will showcase how this formulation enables successful attacks, proving that causal structure learning, generalized linear models, and causal inference frameworks are all significantly susceptible to strategically engineered missingness.
talks.short_abstract: A study of adversarial missingness attacks showing that missing-data manipulation can significantly weaken causal and statistical learning systems.

talks.speaker: Sadia Asif
talks.title: Optimization-driven Framework for Machine Unlearning
talks.abstract: Large language models deployed in sensitive applications increasingly require the ability to unlearn specific knowledge, such as user requests, copyrighted materials, or outdated information, without retraining from scratch to ensure regulatory compliance, user privacy, and safety. This task, known as machine unlearning, aims to remove the influence of targeted data (forgetting) while maintaining performance on the remaining data (retention). A common approach is to formulate this as a multi-objective problem and reduce it to a single-objective problem via scalarization, where forgetting and retention losses are combined using a weighted sum. However, this often results in unstable training dynamics and degraded model utility due to conflicting gradient directions. To address these challenges, we propose OFMU, a penalty-based bi-level optimization framework that explicitly prioritizes forgetting while preserving retention through a hierarchical structure. Our method enforces forgetting via an inner maximization step that incorporates a similarity-aware penalty to decorrelate the gradients of the forget and retention objectives and restores utility through an outer minimization step. To ensure scalability, we develop a two-loop algorithm with provable convergence guarantees under both convex and non-convex regimes. We further provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of convergence rates and show that our approach achieves better trade-offs between forgetting efficacy and model utility compared to prior methods.
talks.short_abstract: A bi-level optimization framework for machine unlearning that improves the forgetting-retention tradeoff and comes with convergence guarantees.

talks.speaker: Hoai-an Nguyen
talks.title: Numerical Linear Algebra in Linear Space
talks.abstract: We present a randomized linear-space solver for general linear systems \(A x = b\) where \(A\) and \(b\) are over the integers and without any assumption on the condition number of \(A\). For matrices whose entries are bounded by \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\), the solver returns a \(1 + \epsilon\)-multiplicative entry-wise approximation to rational vector \(x\) using \(\tilde{O}(n^2 \cdot \operatorname{nnz}(A))\) bit operations and \(O(n \log n)\) bits of working space, where \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) denotes the number of nonzero entries. To our knowledge, this is the first linear-space linear system solver over the rationals that runs in \(\tilde{O}(n^2 \cdot \operatorname{nnz}(A))\) time. We also present several applications of our solver to numerical linear algebra problems, for which we provide algorithms with efficient polynomial running time and near-linear space. In particular, we present results for linear regression, linear programming, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and singular value decomposition.
talks.short_abstract: A randomized linear-space solver for \(A x = b\), with applications to regression, LP, and spectral problems.

talks.speaker: Khai Dong
talks.title: Label Complexity of Linear Regression
talks.abstract: Given a known system matrix \(X\) with \(n\) rows corresponding to experiments whose outputs \(y\) are costly to obtain, how can we selectively pay to observe only a fraction of the entries of \(y\) despite making no assumptions about \(y\) while ensuring that the resulting estimator incurs only a small multiplicative increase in error? This RQE talk will survey algorithms and guarantees for doing this efficiently in the worst case over \(y\).
talks.short_abstract: A survey of label-efficient linear regression methods for estimating \(y\) from a known system matrix \(X\) with few costly observations.

talks.speaker: Xingjian Zhao
talks.title: WIN-U: Woodbury-Informed Newton-Unlearning as a retain-free Machine Unlearning Framework
talks.abstract: Privacy concerns in LLMs have led to the rapidly growing need to enforce a data's right to be forgotten. Machine unlearning addresses precisely this task, namely the removal of the influence of some specific data, i.e., the forget set, from a trained model. The gold standard for unlearning is to produce the model that would have been learned on only the rest of the training data, i.e., the retain set. Most existing unlearning methods rely on direct access to the retained data, which may not be practical due to privacy or cost constraints. We propose WIN-U, a retained-data free unlearning framework that requires only second-order information for the originally trained model on the full data. The unlearning is performed using a single Newton-style step. Using the Woodbury matrix identity and a generalized Gauss-Newton approximation for the forget set curvature, the WIN-U update recovers the closed-form linear solution and serves as a local second-order approximation to the gold-standard retraining optimum. Extensive experiments on various vision and language benchmarks demonstrate that WIN-U achieves SOTA performance in terms of unlearning efficacy and utility preservation, while being more robust against relearning attacks compared to existing methods. Importantly, WIN-U does not require access to the retained data.
talks.short_abstract: A retain-free machine unlearning framework using a single Newton-style step and second-order information.

talks.speaker: Yuxuan Zhu
talks.title: SentenceKV: Efficient LLM Inference via Sentence-Level Semantic KV Caching
talks.abstract: Large language models struggle with memory and computation when handling long contexts. Efficient key-value (KV) cache management is essential for reducing overhead during inference. We introduce SentenceKV, a sentence-level semantic KV caching method that improves efficiency while maintaining coherence. Extensive evaluations on benchmarks including PG-19, LongBench, Needle-In-A-Haystack, and RULER demonstrate that SentenceKV significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both efficiency and memory usage, without compromising model accuracy.
talks.short_abstract: A sentence-level semantic KV caching method that improves LLM inference efficiency without hurting accuracy.

talks.speaker: Duc Khai Dong
talks.title: Tight Success Probabilities for Quantum Period Finding and Phase Estimation
talks.format: in submission, Physica Scripta - practice talk
talks.abstract: Period finding and phase estimation are fundamental in quantum computing. Prior work has established lower bounds on their success probabilities. Such quantum algorithms measure a state \(\lvert\hat{\ell}\rangle\) in an \(n\)-qubit computational basis, with \(\hat{\ell}\in[0,2^n-1]\), and then post-process this measurement to produce the final output; in the case of period finding, a divisor of the period \(r\). We consider a general post-processing algorithm that succeeds whenever the measured \(\hat{\ell}\) is within some tolerance \(M\) of a positive integer multiple of \(2^n/r\). We give new tight lower and upper bounds on the success probability that converge to \(1\). The parameter \(n\) captures the complexity of the quantum circuit. The parameter \(M\) can be tuned by varying the post-processing algorithm (for example, by adding brute-force search or lattice methods). Our tight analysis allows for the careful exploitation of tradeoffs between the complexity of the quantum circuit and the effort spent in classical processing when optimizing the probability of success. We note that the most recent prior work (Ekerå, 2024) does not give tight bounds for general \(M\).
talks.short_abstract: Tight bounds for the success probability of quantum period finding and phase estimation as a function of \(\hat{\ell}\), \(n\), \(M\), and \(r\).

talks.speaker: Yuanzhe Liu
talks.title: Lessons Learned: A Multi-Agent Framework for Code LLMs to Learn and Improve
talks.abstract: Recent studies show that LLMs possess different skills and specialize in different tasks. In fact, we observe that their varied performance occurs at several levels of granularity. For example, in the code optimization task, code LLMs excel at different optimization categories and no one dominates the others. This observation prompts the question of how one leverages multiple LLM agents to solve a coding problem without knowing their complementary strengths a priori. We argue that a team of agents can learn from each other's successes and failures so as to improve their own performance. Thus, a lesson is the knowledge produced by an agent and passed on to other agents in the collective solution process. We propose a lesson-based collaboration framework, design the lesson solicitation-banking-selection mechanism, and demonstrate that a team of small LLMs with lessons learned can outperform a much larger LLM and other multi-LLM collaboration methods.
talks.short_abstract: A multi-agent collaboration framework where agents exchange lessons from successes and failures to improve code LLM performance.

talks.speaker: Lia Zhang
talks.title: Diagnosing and Addressing Pitfalls in KG-RAG Datasets: Toward More Reliable Benchmarking
talks.abstract: Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) systems rely on high-quality benchmarks to evaluate complex multi-hop reasoning. However, despite their widespread use, popular datasets such as WebQSP and CWQ suffer from critical quality issues, including inaccurate or incomplete ground-truth annotations, poorly constructed questions that are ambiguous, trivial, or unanswerable, and outdated or inconsistent knowledge. Through a manual audit of 16 popular KGQA datasets, including WebQSP and CWQ, we find that the average factual correctness rate is only 57\%. To address these issues, we introduce KGQAGen, an LLM-in-the-loop framework that systematically resolves these pitfalls. KGQAGen combines structured knowledge grounding, LLM-guided generation, and symbolic verification to produce challenging and verifiable QA instances. Using KGQAGen, we construct KGQAGen-10k, a ten-thousand-scale benchmark grounded in Wikidata, and evaluate a diverse set of KG-RAG models. Experimental results demonstrate that even state-of-the-art systems struggle on this benchmark, highlighting its ability to expose limitations of existing models. Our findings advocate for more rigorous benchmark construction and position KGQAGen as a scalable framework for advancing KGQA evaluation.
talks.short_abstract: A benchmark-auditing and data-generation framework that exposes weaknesses in KGQA and KG-RAG datasets.

talks.speaker: Maruf Mridul
talks.title: LLM & RAG-Powered Encoding of Financial Derivative Contracts
talks.abstract: This work presents a framework for automating the transformation and optimization of financial derivative contracts using Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and Reinforcement Learning (RL). The framework first uses LLMs and RAG to convert unstructured Over-the-Counter (OTC) derivative contracts into structured Common Domain Model (CDM) representations, ensuring syntactic correctness and schema compliance. Subsequently, an RL agent is employed to generate gas-efficient smart contracts directly from CDM specifications. The agent is trained in two phases: first, to ensure successful compilation, and then to minimize gas costs, achieving significant reductions in deployment and execution expenses. This approach enables the automated creation of both functionally correct and economically optimized smart contracts, facilitating efficient on-chain execution of financial agreements.
talks.short_abstract: A pipeline that converts OTC derivative contracts into CDM representations and then into gas-efficient smart contracts.

talks.speaker: Fernando Spadea
talks.title: Enhancing Recommendation Systems using Large Language Models and Personalized Knowledge Graphs
talks.abstract: We investigate how large language models (LLMs), when paired with personalized knowledge graphs (PKGs), can power decentralized recommendation systems. This work lays the groundwork for more intelligent and user-aligned personal digital assistants that respect user autonomy and data sovereignty. A key focus of our research is exploring how LLMs can be fine-tuned in federated settings to balance personalization with privacy. To this end, we evaluate several fine-tuning methods and compare their performance to select the best one. Early results indicate that LLMs fine-tuned to use PKGs can outperform symbolic and embedding-based KGC models (e.g., KBGAT, HAKE) in both centralized and federated contexts, and that fine-tuning with Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) is more resilient to lopsided data distributions.
talks.short_abstract: LLMs paired with personalized knowledge graphs can improve decentralized recommendation while preserving privacy and autonomy.

talks.speaker: Alex Gittens
talks.title: Learning Under Corruption: Iterative Thresholding in the Strong Contamination Model
talks.abstract: Machine learning systems are often trained on data that are messy, mislabeled, or even maliciously corrupted. The strong contamination model captures this most difficult regime, allowing an adversary to arbitrarily alter an \(\epsilon\)-fraction of both features and labels. It provides a powerful lens for understanding how algorithms behave when data quality cannot be guaranteed. This talk introduces simple, gradient-based iterative thresholding methods that remain effective even under such severe corruption. By discarding the most inconsistent samples during training, these algorithms can reliably learn linear and nonlinear predictors such as ReLU and leaky-ReLU neurons, with provable accuracy \(O(\sigma\epsilon\log(1/\epsilon))\) and faster runtimes than prior approaches. The results highlight that robustness to the worst data failures can be achieved through surprisingly lightweight techniques.
talks.short_abstract: Iterative thresholding under the strong contamination model yields lightweight robustness guarantees for corrupted learning problems.

talks.speaker: Yue Gruszecki
talks.title: Compatibility of Max and Sum Objectives for Committee Selection and k-Facility Location
talks.abstract: We study a version of the metric facility location problem (or, equivalently, variants of the committee selection problem) in which we must choose \(k\) facilities in an arbitrary metric space to serve some set of clients \(C\). We consider four different objectives, where each client \(i \in C\) attempts to minimize either the sum or the maximum of its distance to the chosen facilities, and where the overall objective either considers the sum or the maximum of the individual client costs. Rather than optimizing a single objective at a time, we study how compatible these objectives are with each other, and show the existence of solutions which are simultaneously close to optimum for any pair of the above objectives. Our results show that when choosing a set of facilities or a representative committee, it is often possible to form a solution which is good for several objectives at the same time, instead of sacrificing one desideratum to achieve another.
talks.short_abstract: A compatibility analysis for committee selection and \(k\)-facility location showing that max and sum objectives can be simultaneously near-optimal.

talks.speaker: Cameron Moy
talks.title: Roulette: A Language for Expressive, Exact, and Efficient Discrete Probabilistic Programming
talks.abstract: Exact probabilistic inference is a requirement for many applications of probabilistic programming languages (PPLs), such as high-consequence settings or verification. However, designing and implementing a PPL with scalable high-performance exact inference is difficult: exact inference engines, much like SAT solvers, are intricate low-level programs that are hard to implement. Due to this implementation challenge, PPLs that support scalable exact inference are restrictive and lack many features of general-purpose languages. This talk presents Roulette, the first discrete probabilistic programming language that combines high-performance exact inference with general-purpose language features. The key insight is that there is a close connection between exact probabilistic inference and the symbolic evaluation strategy of Rosette. Building on this connection, Roulette generalizes and extends the Rosette solver-aided programming system to reason about probabilistic rather than symbolic quantities.
talks.short_abstract: A discrete probabilistic programming language that combines exact inference with general-purpose language features.
